Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 49, verse 1:

Medinan, and its verses number 18 [revealed after al-Mujadila]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

*Qaddamahu* and *aqdamahu*: both are transmitted forms, with the intensive doubling of the middle radical and with the hamza, from *qaddama* (to go before) when one goes ahead of him, as in His saying ﴿يَقْدُمُ قَوْمَهُ﴾ ("he will go before his people"). Their counterparts in meaning and transmission are *salafahu* and *aslafahu*. As for His saying ﴿لا تُقَدِّمُوا﴾ ("Do not put forward") without an object stated, there are two possibilities. The first is that the object is omitted so that it covers everything that may occur to the mind as something to be put forward. The second is that no object is intended and none is omitted, and the prohibition is directed at the act of putting forward itself, as if it were said: do not go ahead into engaging in this act, and do not make it a path for yourselves, like His saying ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي يُحْيِي وَيُمِيتُ﴾ ("It is He who gives life and causes death").

[Al-Zamakhshari cites from the Nukat: "He, exalted is He, opened the surah by requiring that the matter which is referred to Allah and His Messenger be placed before all other matters, without restriction or specification." Ahmad says: he means that the object which "tuqaddimu" would require was not mentioned, the object being left out, like His saying ﴿يُحْيِي وَيُمِيتُ﴾; and the speech is embellished with the figurative mode of imagery in His saying ﴿بَيْنَ يَدَيِ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ﴾ with a benefit not found in plain speech, namely the depicting of the ugliness and abomination of what they were forbidden: acting on a matter without following the models of the Book and the Sunnah. The image of what is forbidden is like a slave sitting in the two directions facing his master's right and left, turning his back to him. Its meaning: do not go ahead on any matter until Allah and His Messenger permit it, so that you are guided in what you do and leave undone by the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet.]

It is permissible that *qaddama* be in the sense of *taqaddama*, as *wajaha* and *bayyana* (in the sense of *tawajjaha* and *tabayyana*). From this comes *muqaddimat al-jaysh* (the vanguard of the army), the opposite of its rearguard, being the group that goes ahead of it. Supporting this is the reading of those who read *lā tuqaddimū* by omitting one of the two *tā'*s of *tatqaddamū*. However, the first is more beautiful in eloquence and more correct, more fitting to the eloquence of the Qur'an, and the scholars incline more to it.

It has also been read *lā taqdamū* from *al-qudūm* (arrival), meaning: do not hasten to a matter of the religion before its arrival, and do not be hasty concerning them.

The literal sense of the expression "I sat between the hands of so-and-so" is that one sits between the two directions facing his right and left, close to him. The two directions were called "two hands" because they lie in the direction of the hands, with nearness to them, as a broadening of usage, just as a thing is named by the name of another when it neighbours it and draws near to it in some respect. This expression has here been used in the manner of a kind of figurative speech, which the rhetoricians call *tamthīl* (the figure of image-depiction). Its being used in this way carries a great benefit not found in plain speech: it is the depicting of the ugliness and abomination of what they were forbidden, namely acting on any matter without following the models of the Book and the Sunnah. The meaning is: do not decide a matter except after they have judged it and permitted it, so that you are either acting upon the revealed Revelation or following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). On this the interpretation of Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) turns. From Mujahid: do not presume upon Allah anything until it is related through the tongue of His Messenger.

It is also permissible that it take the course of your saying: "Zayd pleased me and his good condition," or "I was impressed by ʿAmr and his generosity." The benefit of this style is to indicate the strength of particular distinction. Since the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) held the station with Allah that is not hidden, this course was taken with him. In this there is a preparation and preface for what He censured them for in what follows of raising their voices above his voice, because whoever Allah has favoured with this distinction and singled out with this strong particularity, the least that is owed to him of reverence and veneration is that one lower one's voice in his presence and speak softly to him.

It was said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a detachment of twenty-seven men to Tihama, with al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr al-Sāʿidī in command, and the Banu ʿAmir killed them, led by ʿAmir ibn al-Tufayl, except for three men who escaped and met two men from the Banu Sulaym near Medina. They claimed to them that they belonged to the Banu ʿAmir, because they were more honourable than the Banu Sulaym, so they killed the two and stripped them. Then they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "What you did was evil; they were from Sulaym, and the spoils are what you clothed them with." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then paid their blood-money. [Al-Bayhaqi related it in al-Shuʿab in the fifteenth section, by way of Muqatil ibn Hayyan who said: "It reached us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a detachment and appointed over them al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr," and he related the story of the Well of Maʿuna at length, and this wording is in it. And in al-Dala'il, by way of Ibn Ishaq, and by way of Musa ibn ʿUqba, the story is given in a different form, and that the slain were of the Banu Kilab, and that of the three one was killed. This is the preserved and well-known version in the campaigns (maghazi).] And it was revealed, meaning: do not act on anything of your own accord until you seek the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

From Masruq: I entered upon ʿA'isha on the day of doubt, and she said to the slave-girl: "Give him honey to drink." I said: "I am fasting." She said: "Allah has forbidden fasting this day." [Al-Tha'labi mentioned this without a chain. Al-Daraqutni mentioned it from the narration of Malik ibn Hamza, from Masruq, who said: "I entered upon ʿA'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) on the day regarding which there is doubt whether it is the Day of ʿArafa..." the hadith.] And this verse was revealed concerning it.

From al-Hasan: some people slaughtered on the day of Eid al-Adha before the prayer, so it was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered them to repeat the slaughter. [ʿAbd al-Razzaq related it: Ma'mar narrated to us from al-Hasan concerning His saying ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تُقَدِّمُوا بَيْنَ يَدَيِ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ﴾, he said: "They were a people who slaughtered before the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed, so he ordered them to repeat the slaughter." Al-Tabari related it from the narration of Said from Qatada, who said: "It was mentioned to us that some people used to say: 'If only such-and-such had been revealed, if only such-and-such were done, if only such-and-such were accepted.'" He said: al-Hasan said: "They were people..." and he mentioned it.] This is the view of Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him), except that the sun must have declined. According to al-Shafiʿi, slaughter is permitted once a period equal to the prayer has passed from the time.

Also from al-Hasan: when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) settled in Medina, delegations came to him from every horizon and they increased their questions to him, so they were forbidden to begin with a question to him until he himself begins. [I have not found it.] From Qatada: it was mentioned to us that some people used to say: "If such-and-such had been revealed concerning it, it would have been such-and-such," so Allah disliked that from them and revealed this.

It was also said: it is general in every saying and action. It includes that if a question arises in the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they should not anticipate him with the answer; that one should not walk in front of him except for a need; and that one should wait before beginning the meal [i.e., wait for the signal to begin].

﴿وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ﴾ ("And fear Allah"): for if you fear Him, your taqwa will restrain you from the forbidden putting-forward and from everything that the watchfulness of Allah requires you to avoid. For the one who fears is cautious and does not occupy himself with a matter except after the doubt is lifted and the uncertainty cleared as to whether he will be held accountable for it. This is like when you say to someone who is committing some vile deeds: "Do not do this, and guard yourself from what brings shame upon you," so you first forbid him from the very thing he is engaged in, then you generalize and extend, and command him with what, if he obeyed your command in it, he would not commit that act, and with everything that lies along its path and is connected to its cause. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ لما تقولون عَلِيمٌ بما تعملون﴾ ("Indeed Allah is All-Hearing of what you say, All-Knowing of what you do"), and such a thing deserves to be guarded against and watched.

﴿Repeating the call to them﴾ is a summons from Him to renew their insight at every divine address that comes down, to refresh their attentiveness to every ruling that is revealed, and to stir them so that they do not slacken or become heedless in their reflection. It also concerns the courtesy they were to observe when attending the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), a courtesy whose preservation brings them great benefit in their religion. This is because honouring the Lawgiver (ṣāḥib al-sharʿ, the one who brings the revealed law) entails honouring what he brought. One who holds the truth in great esteem will not, through that esteem, neglect to strive in acting upon what urges him to it, and to refrain from what turns him away from it, and to reach every good.

As for His saying ﴿Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾, its meaning is this: when he speaks and you speak, you must not let your voices rise beyond the limit to which he raises his voice. You must lower your voices so that his speech is higher than your speech and his loudness is conspicuous above your loudness, so that his distinction over you is evident, his precedence is clear, and his distinction from your assembly is as obvious as the piebald horse's markings (kashshiyat al-ablaq) [[His saying "kashshiyat al-ablaq": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "al-shiyya" is a colour that differs from the main colour of a horse or other animal. Also in it: "al-laghṭ" is voice and clamour, and "al-ṣakhab" is shouting and clamour. (Ibn Ḥajar? — the gloss marked (ʿ) in the source.)]]. He must not be drowned out by your din, nor his speech overwhelmed by your clamour.

And by His saying ﴿and do not speak loudly to him﴾: if you address him while he is silent, beware of departing from what you were forbidden, namely raising the voice. Rather, you must not carry your voices to the loudness that circulates among you, and you must deliberately adopt in addressing him a gentle speech approaching a whisper, which is the opposite of loudness, just as one addresses a revered and magnified person, acting upon His saying, ﴿and that you honour him and revere him﴾.

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿and do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another﴾ is: do not say to him, "O Muhammad! O Ahmad!" but address him with prophethood (i.e., with the title of Prophet). Ibn ʿAbbas said: when this verse was revealed, Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, I will not speak to you except as one who whispers, or like the brother of one who whispers, until I meet Allah." [[Al-Wahidi mentioned it from ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās, but did not give its chain to him. Al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it through Ṭāriq ibn Shihāb from Abu Bakr, who said: "When it was revealed, ﴿O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾, I said: O Messenger of Allah, I have sworn that I will not speak to you except as the brother of one who whispers, until I meet Allah." Al-Ḥākim and al-Bayhaqī in al-Madkhal also transmitted it from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: "When ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices﴾ was revealed, Abu Bakr said: By Him who sent down the Book upon you, O Messenger of Allah, I will not speak to you except as the brother of one who whispers, until I meet Allah the Mighty and Majestic." Al-Ḥākim said: it is sound according to the condition of Muslim.]] And from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him): he used to speak to the Prophet (ﷺ) as the brother of one who whispers, not being heard until he was asked to repeat himself. [[Al-Bukhārī transmitted it from the hadith of Abu al-Zubayr, who said: "When ﴿O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ was revealed, ʿUmar after that, when he spoke to the Prophet (ﷺ), would speak to him like the brother of one who whispers; he was not heard until he was asked to repeat himself."]] And Abu Bakr, whenever a delegation came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), would send to them someone to teach them how to greet, and would command them to tranquillity and gravity in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). [[I have not found it.]]

The purpose of raising the voice and of loudness is not what is intended to show contempt and disdain, for that is disbelief, and those addressed are believers. Rather, the intent is a voice which, in itself and in the sound that is heard from it, is not suitable for what great men are revered for and noble men are honoured by, so that one feels compelled to lower it and bring it back to a limit that inclines it toward what makes plain the commanded reverence and honour. The prohibition does not also cover raising the voice in a way that does not harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), such as what they did in war, in disputation with a stubborn opponent, in frightening an enemy, or the like. In a hadith, he (ﷺ) said to al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib when the people fled on the day of Ḥunayn: "Call out to the people." [[I have not found it. It has been mentioned earlier that this was on the day of Ḥunayn, and al-ʿAbbās did not witness anyone (i.e., the report is doubtful).]] Al-ʿAbbās was the loudest of people in voice. [[I have not found it.]] It is narrated that once a raid came upon them, and al-ʿAbbās cried out, "O morning-alarm!" so that pregnant women miscarried because of the intensity of his voice. [[I have not found it.]] Concerning this, the poet Nābigha of Banū Jaʿda said:

"The roar of Abu ʿUrwa driving off the beasts of prey, when he feared they would mix with the sheep."

[[The explanation of this verse was given earlier in this volume on page 38, so refer to it if you wish. (Note by its corrector.)]]

The transmitters claimed that he would drive the beasts of prey away from the sheep, and the predator's gall would burst within it. [[I have not found it.]]

In the reading of Ibn Masʿūd: ﴿do not raise your bi-aṣwātikum (with your voices)﴾, the bāʾ being superfluous and used in the manner of the doubling in the verse of al-Aʿlam al-Hudhalī:

"I raised my eyes with the Ḥijāz toward people in the Manāqib."

[[Of al-A'lam al-Hudhali, who says: "I looked, while I was in the Hijaz, toward those who are in al-Manaqib." These two places are far apart, and this is from the intensity of longing for those who are in al-Manaqib.]]

The meaning in this reading is not that they were forbidden from intense raising, under the supposition that what falls short of intense raising would be permissible to them. Rather, the meaning is a prohibition of the clamour they were engaged in and of the coarseness they displayed in what they used to do.

It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that it was revealed concerning Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammās. He was hard of hearing and had a loud voice, so whenever he spoke he raised his voice, and sometimes he would speak to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Messenger would be harmed by his voice. [[I have not found it.]]

It is also reported from Anas that when this verse was revealed, Thābit was absent, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked after him and was informed of his condition. He summoned him, and asked him, and he said: "O Messenger of Allah, this verse has been revealed to you, and I am a man of loud voice, and I fear that my deeds have been nullified." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "You are not in that state; you will live in goodness and die in goodness, and you are of the people of Paradise." [[Agreed upon (Bukhārī and Muslim) from the hadith of Anas, except for his saying "You are not in that state." Aḥmad and al-Ṭabarānī added in it: Anas said, "We used to see him walking among us, and we knew that he was of the people of Paradise."]]

As for what is reported from al-Ḥasan, that it was revealed concerning those hypocrites who raised their voices above the voice of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), its interpretation, with the address being to the believers, is that the believers are forbidden so that the hypocrites fall under the prohibition, making the matter more severe and more burdensome for them. It has also been said: the hypocrites used to raise their voices to show their indifference, so that the weak among the Muslims would follow them.

The particle of comparison (kāf al-tashbīh) is in a position of accusative case, meaning: do not speak loudly to him with loudness like the loudness of some of you to others. In this it is shown that they were not forbidden from loudness absolutely, so that it would not be permissible for them to speak to him except in a whisper and in a low voice; rather they were forbidden a particular loudness restricted by an attribute, namely the loudness described as resembling what they had become accustomed to among themselves, which is the absence of regard for the dignity of prophethood and the magnitude of its rank, and the lowering of all other ranks even if they are exalted beyond its rank.

﴿lest your deeds be nullified﴾ is in the accusative position, as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu). It has two possible points of attachment. One: it attaches to the sense of the prohibition, so the meaning is: "Desist from what you were forbidden, for fear that your deeds be nullified," i.e., for fear of their nullification, with the noun (al-muḍāf, "fear") omitted, like His saying, ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾. The second: it attaches to the act itself, and the meaning is that they were forbidden from the act they performed for the sake of nullification, because since it was on the path to leading to nullification, it was treated as though it were done for its sake, and as though nullification were its cause and reason for its existence, by way of figurative speech, like His saying, ﴿so that they might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾.

[Al-Zamakhsharī said:] "If you say: summarize the difference between the two views? I say: its summary is that in the second one, the act is assumed to be joined with the object of purpose, as if they were one thing. [[Maḥmūd said: "It is an object of purpose, and its attachment is either the sense of the prohibition, as if he said: 'Desist, out of aversion to the nullification of your deeds,' with an omitted noun, like His saying ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾. As for the act itself, it is what is forbidden, in the sense of the transformation of the loudness that is forbidden into nullification, treated as the placing of nullification as the cause of loudness, by way of figurative speech, of the type of ﴿so that they might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾. He said: The difference between them is that in the second one, one assumes the joining of the object of purpose to the first verb ... etc."

Aḥmad said: He is circling around the doctrine and bias of "Beware" (iyyāka) and its arrival. This is because he holds that anything less than disbelief, even a single major sin, nullifies the deed and necessitates eternal abiding in the lasting punishment, and removes the believer from the name and trace of faith. Far be it from Allah that this belief be held. So hold fast to the established creed of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the followers of the prophetic tradition) that is laid out in several places in this collection, and renew your pledge to it: it is the belief that the believer does not abide forever in the Fire, that Paradise is his by the absolute promise of Allah even if his sins are other than polytheism or what leads to it, even as many as the foam of the sea, and that no good deed is nullified by any sin that occurs, whatever it is, except polytheism.

And al-Zamakhsharī seized the opportunity in the outward meaning of this verse, interpreting it according to his doctrine, and the aspect of its apparent meaning in what he claims is this: raising the voice in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is a disobedience that does not reach polytheism, and Allah has frightened His servants with the nullification of their deeds by it. If nullification were definitively negated, the frightening by it would not be sound. How could he reach his hopes in that? The structure of the speech rejects it according to the insight of its meaning. So we say: what is meant in the verse is the prohibition of raising the voice absolutely. It is known that the ruling of a prohibition is caution against what is anticipated from it of harming the Prophet, peace be upon him. The chosen principle is that harming him, peace be upon him, reaches the level of disbelief which nullifies deeds by consensus. So the prohibition came concerning what is likely to be a harm to the Prophet, peace be upon him, whether or not this meaning is present initially, as a protection of the means and a closing of the source. Then, since this prohibited thing, which is raising the voice, is divided into what reaches that level and what does not, and there is no evidence distinguishing one of the two divisions from the other, it became binding on the responsible person to refrain from it absolutely, and it was feared that he might fall into either of the two, the one that nullifies deeds, which is that reaching the limit of harm, since no clear evidence distinguishes it. If there were such evidence, its distinction would not be achieved in many cases. And it is to the confusion of one division with the other that the allusion was made in His saying, ﴿lest your deeds be nullified while you do not perceive﴾. Otherwise, if the matter were as Zamakhsharī believes, His saying ﴿while you do not perceive﴾ would have no place, since the matter is between raising the voice being harmful, in which case it is definitely disbelief that nullifies, and between it not being harmful, in which case it is a major sin that nullifies, according to his opinion, definitely. So in both of its states the nullification by it is certain. Therefore there is no place for reinforcing the speech by the non-perception, while nullification is established absolutely. And Allah knows best. This explanation I have mentioned rests on two premises, both of which are sound. The first: raising the voice is of the kind by which harm is caused, and this is a matter attested by transmission and by present observation, to the extent that a teacher is harmed by a student raising his voice before him, so how much more the rank of prophethood and what it deserves of glorification and exaltation. The second premise: harming the Prophet (ﷺ) is disbelief, and this is a established matter that our imams have stated explicitly, and they have issued rulings that whoever does that is to be killed as a disbeliever, and his repentance is not accepted. So what he does is greater and more grave with Allah. And Allah is the Granter of success.]], then He pours the prohibition upon both of them entirely. In the first, the prohibition is directed at the act on its own, and then its reason is given for the thing forbidden. If you say: with which of the two prohibitions is the object of purpose connected?

I say: with the second according to the Basrans, its implied pronoun being assumed in the first, like His saying, ﴿Bring me, I will pour over it molten brass﴾. And the reverse according to the Kufans. Whichever it is, the meaning returns to this: both raising and loudness have been stated to lead to the nullification of deeds. The reading of Ibn Masʿūd, "so that your deeds are nullified" (fa-taḥbaṭa aʿmālukum), is more explicit in this, because what follows the fāʾ (fa) is only the consequence of what precedes it. So the nullification from loudness descends to the position of the descent of "settling" from "transgression" in His saying, ﴿so that My wrath settles upon you﴾. "Ḥubūṭ" (nullification) is from ḥabiṭat al-ibil, when camels eat green plants and their bellies swell, and they sometimes die. And from this is His, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "Indeed, among what spring grass grows is that which kills by bloating or by sickness." [[Transmitted by Muslim and others.]] Among its cognates is ḥabijat al-ibil, when camels eat ʿarfaj and are afflicted by it. And aḥbaṭa ʿamalahu means the same as aḥbaṭahu. And ḥabaṭa al-jurḥ wa-ḥabar means when a wound festers, and it is its sickening and its spreading toward corruption. The evil deed in its harm to the good deed is treated like a disease and a debilitation (ḥaraḍ) for whoever is afflicted by it. [[His saying "a disease and a debilitation": that is, corruption, as the Ṣiḥāḥ states.]] May Allah protect us from the nullification of deeds and the disappointment of hopes.

The verse has indicated two terrifying matters. The first: that among the sins committed by a believer is that which nullifies his deed. The second: that among his sins is that which he does not know to be nullifying, and perhaps it is so with Allah. So the believer must be, in his piety, like one walking along a thorny path, who never ceases to be cautious, to guard against, and to be watchful.

﴿God has tested their hearts for piety﴾. This is from your saying: "So-and-so was tested (imtahana) for such-and-such a matter, and was trained and practised (wa-jurriba) for it, and was drilled (wa-darraba) for undertaking it." Thus he is capable of bearing it and does not weaken from it. The meaning is that they are patient in piety and strong in bearing its hardships.

Or the testing is placed in the position of knowledge, because the establishing of a thing is through testing it, just as the report is placed in the position of knowledge. It is as if it were said: "God knew their hearts for piety." The lam (al-lam) is then connected to an omitted element, and this lam is the one in your saying: "You are for this matter" (anta li-hadha al-amr), meaning: it belongs to him and is specific to him. The poet said:

*You are fit for it, the most praiseworthy among mankind*

The line is excellent, free of superfluity and complexity. Its form (sawghatuha), with the doubled letter, is for emphasis. "Anta lahā" means: you are qualified for it and equal to it. "Aḥmad" is a vocative noun (munada). "Min bayn al-bashar" is connected to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial qualifier, meaning: chosen from among them. It is said that "aḥmad" may be an elative (af'al al-tafdil), as has been said.

*O Ada, for whom the camels that work hard on the hoofs' wounds are prepared,*
*and the guests of a house that spent the night waiting for the arrival (of the caravan)*

*O Ada, for whom life holds no pleasure after you,*
*and no friend has joy in friendship.*

*O Ada, my grief for you is not light,*
*nor is patience, if it were granted, beautiful.*

This is by Utba ibn Malik al-Uqayli, lamenting his companion Ada. The hamza is for the vocative. "Ada," in the pattern of *fa'al* (intensive form), means: O you who were ready to aid the camels that labour greatly, and who travelled with the *wija'* (the soreness of the hoofs from much walking). The *ya'milat* is the plural of *ya'mala*, and the camel is called *ya'mal*. He was also ready for the guests of his house who spent the night there to rest and lodge with him. "Al-'aysh" means life, or that by which one lives. "Al-bahja" means joy. "Al-wajd" means grief. "In a'tayhi" is a parenthetical clause, showing that he did not endure patiently. The negation of the beauty of patience is an exaggeration of the greatness of Ada's position and his love for him. He repeated the vocative to express lamentation.

The phrase, together with what it governs, is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). Or God struck their hearts with various kinds of trials and difficult obligations for the sake of piety, meaning so that its (piety's) steadfastness and manifestation would become evident, and so that it would be known that they are pious, because the reality of piety is not known except at times of trial and hardship and steadfastness in them. It has also been said that He purified their hearts for piety. This is from the saying: "He tested the gold and refined it" (imtahana al-dhahab wa-fatanahu), when he melted it and separated its pure essence from its dross and cleansed it. It is reported from ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "He removed desires from them."

*Imtihan* is a *ifti'al* form, from *mahana*, which is a severe test or a grievous affliction. Abu ʿAmr said: "Everything you have exhausted, you have *mahantahu*." He recited:

*The exhausted she-camels came, their weariness visible,*
*they had been tried, and their flanks were trembling.*

*Al-radhaya* is the plural of *radhiyya*, which is the lean, weak she-camel. *Mahantuhu* means I tested him. It is said: "I tried my she-camel" (mahantu naqati), meaning I exhausted her in travel. "Mahantu al-jild" means I stretched and widened the hide. *Al-atal* is the plural of *utl*, which is the flank, like *asbab* and *sabab*. He says: the mounts came as emaciated creatures, their weariness and fatigue evident from the journey; those she-camels had been exhausted by travel. Or, their flanks had sagged and trembled from severe hunger. It is also narrated as *awsaluha*, meaning their limbs.

It was said: this verse was revealed concerning the two shaykhs, Abu Bakr and ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both, because of what came from them of lowering their voices and raising them to the point of near-whispering. The structure of this verse, with its arrangement by which those who lower their voices are made the subject of *inna* (ism inna), the emphatic particle...

Its predicate (khabar) is a sentence consisting of a subject and predicate, both definite. The subject is the demonstrative pronoun (ism al-isharah). The resumption of the clause, which contains what their recompense is for their deeds, and the mention of the recompense in indefinite form, its matter being left vague, is to indicate the utmost esteem and approval for what those who honoured the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did by lowering their voices. It also informs of the magnitude of the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) honour and the exalted rank of his station. Within it there is an allusion to the great wrong committed by those who raised their voices, and the deserving of the opposite of what these men deserved.

The wara' (behind): the direction that a person hides from you with his shadow, whether from behind or in front. [Mahmud said: "al-wara' is the direction that a person hides from you with his shadow, whether from behind or in front... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said:]

Some people were deceived into reproaching the Banu Tamim with something the verse does not support. The verse was revealed about those who called out to the Prophet ﷺ, or about those present at that time who approved of the action of those who called out. The Prophet ﷺ was asked about them and said: "They are the boorish Banu Tamim." In general, ﴿no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. How, then, is it permissible to let the tongue loose with evil against a great nation because one or two of them committed folly and boorishness? It has been reported that the one who called out to the Prophet ﷺ was al-Aqra'. This is in addition to the many hadiths that have come down concerning the virtues of Tamim and their perpetuation in the sound books.

The min (from) here indicates the starting point of the end, meaning that the calling originated from that place. If you say: "There is a difference between the two statements, between what it (the particle) is present in and what it is absent from." I say: the difference between them is that the one calling and the one being called, in the first case, can both be encompassed by the wara', whereas in the second case they cannot, because the wara' becomes a starting point of the end when min is added, and one direction cannot be both the starting point and the terminus of a single action. One who says, "So-and-so called me from behind the house," does not mean the front of the house or its back, but any of its visible sides, without specification or restriction. The reproach did not apply to them on the grounds that the calling took place at the back of the rooms or at their fronts; rather, what was condemned was that they called out to him from the open desert [the barriyya] and from outside, the calling out of boors to one another without intending any particular direction.

[The note on "from the open desert and from outside": the apparent sense is that its explanation is what follows it. In al-Sihah, under the root b-r-r, it is stated that al-bariyya is the desert. Under the root d-m-n, in explaining his words, peace be upon him, in one of his letters, "Indeed for us is the al-dahiya of the al-ba'l, and for you the al-damina of the palm trees," the text reads: al-dahiya is the visible one of the palm trees located in the open country, and al-damina is what their cities and villages include. (Ayn)]

The hujura: a plot of land enclosed by a wall that surrounds it, and a camel enclosure is called a hujra. It is of the form fu'la in the sense of maf'ula, like ghurfa and qabda. Its plurals are hujurat (with two dammas), hujarat (with a fatha on the jim), and hujarat (with sukun). All three have been read. The intended meaning is the rooms of the wives of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, each of whom had a room. Their calling out from behind them may mean that they dispersed among the rooms searching for him, so some called out from behind this one and some from behind that one; or that they came to the rooms one by one and called out from behind them; or that they called out from behind the room in which he was, but it was expressed in the plural out of reverence for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and for the sanctity of his position. Although the action is attributed to all of them, it is permissible that only some of them carried it out while the rest approved, so it is as if all of them undertook it. al-Asamm mentioned that the one who called out was 'Uyayna ibn Hisn and al-Aqra' ibn Habis. The statement about most of them, that they do not understand, may include an exception for some of them, or the judgment that the intelligent among them are few may be intended to negate that any of them understands, since paucity is used in their speech in the sense of negation.

It is reported that the delegation of the Banu Tamim came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at midday while he was sleeping, and they began calling out: "Muhammad, come out to us!" He awoke and went out. [Ibn Ishaq reported it in the Sira, saying: "The delegations of the Arabs came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ," and he mentioned the story, and said: "When the delegation of the Banu Tamim arrived, they entered the mosque and called out to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from behind the rooms: 'O Muhammad, come out to us!'" up to the end. Ibn Mardawayh reported it from the narration of Ibn Ishaq, from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When the delegation of the Banu Tamim came, and they were seventy men," and he mentioned it at length. Ibn Mandah also reported it in al-Ma'rifa. al-Tha'labi cited it through the chain of Ya'la ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far, from Shamir ibn al-Hakam, from Jabir, who said: "The Banu Tamim came, entered the mosque, and called out to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from behind the rooms, saying: 'O Muhammad, come out to us!' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was disturbed by their shouting," and he mentioned it at length.] And the verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about them and said: "They are the boorish Banu Tamim. Were it not that they are among the fiercest of people in fighting the one-eyed Dajjal, I would have prayed to Allah against them that He destroy them." [al-Tha'labi reported it through the narration of Hashim ibn al-Qasim al-Harrani, from Ya'la ibn al-Ashdaq, who related from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah that the Prophet ﷺ... and he mentioned it. In Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra: "I shall not cease to love the Banu Tamim for three reasons," and he mentioned in it: "and they are the fiercest of my community against the Dajjal."]

Thus the revelation of the verse in the manner in which it came is clear to anyone who reflects. Among the proofs of the great esteem and honour of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ are: first, the verse came in a form that records against those who shouted at him with foolishness and ignorance what they had undertaken. Second, the word hujurat and its use as a metonymy for the place of his solitude and his midday rest with some of his wives. Third, passing over the word with restraint, limited to the measure by which what was disapproved of them is made clear. Fourth, the definite article being used rather than an idafa (possessive construction). Fifth, that the reproach of them is coupled with their coarseness, the disorder of their minds, and their poor command of the proper places of discernment in speech, so as to make the affair light for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, to console him, and to remove what his being disturbed by their arrogance and bad manners had caused him, and so on from the beginning of the sura to the end of this verse.

Reflect on how it begins with the obligation that matters attributed to Allah and His Messenger should take precedence over all other matters, without limitation or restriction. Then it follows this with the prohibition of what belongs to the same category as precedence, namely raising the voice and speaking loudly. It is as if the first is a carpet for the second and a preparation for it. Then, as a commendation of those who avoided that and lowered their voices, as an indication of his great standing with Allah, there follows what is more grievous and more complete in its reprehensibility: shouting at the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was alone with some of his sacred privacy, from behind the walls, as one shouts at the least esteemed of people. This is done to alert to the heinousness of those who approached him and dared against him. For one whom Allah has elevated to the point that he is addressed in a lowered voice, and even the chiefs of the Muhajirun and the Ansar addressed him as "brother of the night-conversation," the conduct of these people was an evil that had reached the utmost level of foulness. From such matters and their like, the fruits of minds are gathered and the excellences of manners are acquired. It is related from Abu 'Ubayd, whose standing in knowledge, asceticism, and reliability of transmission is well known, that he said: "I never knocked on the door of a scholar but that he came out at the time of his coming out."

[The grammar of "anna hum sabaru":] "Anna hum sabaru" is in the nominative place as the subject, because the meaning is: "Had their patience been established." Al-sabr is restraining the self from pulling toward its desires. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾. The saying "sabara 'an kadha" (he was patient regarding such-and-such) has an omitted object, which is the self, and it is a restraint in which there is severity and hardship for the one restrained. Therefore the restraint upon an oath or execution is called sabr. One of them said: "Patience is bitter; none drinks it except a free man."

If you say: "Is there any difference between ḥattā takhruja (until you come out) and ilā an takhruja (to the point that you come out)?" I say: ḥattā is specific to a stipulated end-point. You say, "I ate the fish until its head," but if you said, "until its half" or "until its chest," it would not be permissible. Ilā is general for every end. So ḥattā, by its very form, conveys that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ's coming out to them was an end set for their patience, and so it was not for them to cut short any matter before reaching it. If you say: "What is the benefit of the phrase ilayhim (to them)?" I say: in it is that if he had come out but his coming out had not been to them and on their account, they would have been obliged to be patient until they knew that his coming out to them was ﴿better for them﴾. The kāna (it was) may be a pronoun for the subject of the verb implied after law (if), or a pronoun for the verbal noun of ṣabarū, as in their saying, "whoever lies, it is worse for him." ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: abundantly forgiving and merciful, of wide scope, so that His forgiveness and mercy will not be too narrow for these people if they repent and turn back in penitence.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 49, verses 6–8:

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent al-Walid ibn Uqba, the half-brother of Uthman through their mother. He was the one whom Uthman had appointed over Kufa after Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. He led the people in the dawn prayer while drunk, performing four rak'ahs, and then said, "Shall I add more for you?" So Uthman dismissed him [[Muslim narrated it through the route of Abu Sasan Husayn ibn al-Mundhir, who said: "I witnessed Uthman, the brother of al-Walid ibn Uqba, when he had led the morning prayer in Kufa with four rak'ahs," and the hadith continues at length. Ibn Ishaq and al-Nasa'i also narrated it by this route, and they said in it, "he led the morning prayer with four rak'ahs."]], and sent him as a collector of zakat to the Banu al-Mustaliq. There was enmity between him and them. When he approached their dwellings, they came out to meet him, and he thought they were coming to fight him. So he turned back and said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, "They have apostatised and withheld zakat." [[Ishaq and al-Tabarani narrated it from the hadith of Umm Salama, without the words "he accused them, and said: 'You must desist, or I will send to you a man who is to me as my own self, who will fight your fighters and take captive your offspring,' etc." In their version, instead of that, it says: "They kept apologising to him until the verse was revealed concerning them." It includes Musa ibn Ubayda, who is weak. A similar report was narrated by Ahmad and al-Tabarani too, from the hadith of al-Harith ibn Dithar al-Khuza'i. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through Abdullah ibn Abd al-Quddus, from al-A'mash, from Musa ibn al-Musayyab, from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent al-Walid ibn Uqba," and he mentioned the hadith in a similar way, adding that the Prayer and peace be upon him said: "You must desist, or I will send to you a man," and he mentioned it.]] Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ became angry and resolved to attack them. The people heard of this, so they came and said, "We seek refuge in Allah from His anger and the anger of His Messenger." Then he accused them, and said: "You must desist, or I will send to you a man who is to me as my own self, who will fight your fighters and take your offspring captive." Then he struck the shoulder of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, with his hand. It was also said: he sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to them, and he found them calling to the prayers and performing night worship, so they handed over the zakat to him, and he returned. [[I have not seen this.]]

As for the indefiniteness (tankir) of "fasiq" (a wrongdoer) and "naba'" (news): it denotes generality (shiya') across all wrongdoers and all reports, as if he said: "Whatever wrongdoer comes to you with whatever news." [[Mahmud said: "He made 'fasiq' and 'naba'' indefinite for the purpose of generality (shiyu'), so it is as if it were said: 'Whatever wrongdoer comes with whatever news.'" Ahmad said: He was lax in using the term shiyu' while meaning inclusiveness (shumul), because an indefinite noun, when it occurs in the context of a conditional, is general, just as when it occurs in the context of negation. And Allah knows best.]] So, when such a person brings news, you should hold back judgment, seek to clarify the matter and uncover the truth, and not rely on the word of the wrongdoer, "for whoever does not avoid the category of wrongdoing does not avoid lying, which is one kind of it."

Al-fusuq (wrongdoing) means to come out of something and strip away from it. It is said: "fasaqat al-rutabah 'an qishriha" (the fresh date came out of its skin). From its inverted form comes: "qafasat al-baydah" (the egg was cracked), when you break it and bring out what is in it. From its inverted form also comes: "qafasat al-shay'," when you take something out of the possession of its owner by usurpation. Then it was used for departing from the intended course and stripping away from the truth.

Ru'ba said:

"Deviating from their intended course, veering aside."

[[The explanation of this witness was given earlier, in the first volume, page 119; refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector.)]]

Ibn Mas'ud recited "fatabayyanu" (so verify) instead of "fatathabbatu." Tathabbut (verification) and tabayyun (clarification) are close in meaning; both mean seeking firmness, clarity, and knowing the facts. Since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and those with him held a rank that no one would dare to tell them a lie, and such a mistake as al-Walid's would happen only rarely, it was said that the conditional "in" (if) with the particle of doubt is used here. [Note: the text says "قيل: إن جاءكم بحرف الشك" which is Zamakhshari's statement that the conditional particle "in" is used, which carries a sense of doubt.] It also implies that the believers should be in this state, so that a wrongdoer will not be tempted to address them with a false word.

"Lest you harm a people in ignorance" (an tusibu qawman bijahalah): the phrase "an tusibu" is an object of purpose, meaning: out of aversion to harming a people in ignorance. "In ignorance" is a circumstantial phrase (hal), like His saying, ﴿And Allah turned back those who disbelieved in their rage﴾ [Q 33:25]. That is, not knowing the reality of the matter or the true nature of the story. The word "isbah" here means "becoming."

Regret (nadam) is a kind of grief. It is that you grieve over what has happened from you, wishing it had not happened. It is a grief that accompanies a person as a constant, lasting companion. Because every time the one who regrets remembers what he regrets, it returns to him. It comes from "nadam," which is the constant companionship of a drinking partner and his enduring company. From its inverted forms comes "adman al-amr" (he persisted in the matter), "adamahu" (he made it constant). And "madan bil-makan" means he stayed in the place. From it comes "al-madinah" (the city). You will find that people make worry a companion, a confidant, a boon-companion, a bedfellow, and describe it as never leaving its companion.

The clause introduced by "law" (if only / had it not been that) cannot be a new, independent statement, because that would lead to a discordance in the structure of the speech. [[Mahmud said: "The clause introduced by 'law' cannot be independent, because that would lead to a discordance in the structure of the speech..." Ahmad said: Among the flaws of the Mu'tazilah is their vilification of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, and their hesitation to rule on the punishment of his killers. To this belief, which they hold without hesitation, is added what al-Zamakhshari brings up in this passage of stories about Uthman's appointing his brother al-Walid, who committed that monstrous act, in place of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, one of the Companions, and what he alludes to, that some Companions would commit faults. Among them was their demanding that the Prophet ﷺ follow their opinions, among which was the acceptance of al-Walid's report about the attack on the Banu al-Mustaliq. If you combine this brief passage with what you know of his creed, what is clear about the state of al-Zamakhshari is something I cannot bring myself to state openly. He did not state it openly, and we have adopted with him the path of fairness and the way of retribution: text for text, allusion for allusion. So we ask Allah, the Mighty, after blessing His Prophet Muhammad, the seal of the prophets, to be pleased with all his Companions, and with us through them. Amin.]] Rather, it is connected to what came before it, as a circumstantial clause (hal) from one of the two pronouns in "fikum" (among you): either the hidden nominative pronoun or the apparent genitive pronoun. Both are sound opinions. The meaning is: "Among you is the Messenger of Allah in a state that you must change," or "You are in a state that you must change, namely that you seek from him to act in events according to what you think, and to consider right the conduct of one who obeys another, following him in his opinion and imitating his example." If he did that, "you would have been in distress," that is, you would have fallen into distress and ruin. It is said: "Fulan ya'attu fulanan," meaning he seeks what leads the other to ruin. And "a'natal 'azm" means the bone was broken after being set.

This indicates that some believers adorned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the idea of attacking the Banu al-Mustaliq and accepting al-Walid's statement.
