There was enmity between him and them. When he approached their dwellings, they came out to meet him, and he thought they were coming to fight him. So he turned back and said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, "They have apostatised and withheld zakat." [[Ishaq and al-Tabarani narrated it from the hadith of Umm Salama, without the words "he accused them, and said: 'You must desist, or I will send to you a man who is to me as my own self, who will fight your fighters and take captive your offspring,' etc." In their version, instead of that, it says: "They kept apologising to him until the verse was revealed concerning them." It includes Musa ibn Ubayda, who is weak. A similar report was narrated by Ahmad and al-Tabarani too, from the hadith of al-Harith ibn Dithar al-Khuza'i. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through Abdullah ibn Abd al-Quddus, from al-A'mash, from Musa ibn al-Musayyab, from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent al-Walid ibn Uqba," and he mentioned the hadith in a similar way, adding that the Prayer and peace be upon him said: "You must desist, or I will send to you a man," and he mentioned it.]] Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ became angry and resolved to attack them. The people heard of this, so they came and said, "We seek refuge in Allah from His anger and the anger of His Messenger." Then he accused them, and said: "You must desist, or I will send to you a man who is to me as my own self, who will fight your fighters and take your offspring captive." Then he struck the shoulder of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, with his hand. It was also said: he sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to them, and he found them calling to the prayers and performing night worship, so they handed over the zakat to him, and he returned. [[I have not seen this.]]

As for the indefiniteness (tankir) of "fasiq" (a wrongdoer) and "naba'" (news): it denotes generality (shiya') across all wrongdoers and all reports, as if he said: "Whatever wrongdoer comes to you with whatever news." [[Mahmud said: "He made 'fasiq' and 'naba'' indefinite for the purpose of generality (shiyu'), so it is as if it were said: 'Whatever wrongdoer comes with whatever news.'" Ahmad said: He was lax in using the term shiyu' while meaning inclusiveness (shumul), because an indefinite noun, when it occurs in the context of a conditional, is general, just as when it occurs in the context of negation. And Allah knows best.]] So, when such a person brings news, you should hold back judgment, seek to clarify the matter and uncover the truth, and not rely on the word of the wrongdoer, "for whoever does not avoid the category of wrongdoing does not avoid lying, which is one kind of it."

Al-fusuq (wrongdoing) means to come out of something and strip away from it. It is said: "fasaqat al-rutabah 'an qishriha" (the fresh date came out of its skin). From its inverted form comes: "qafasat al-baydah" (the egg was cracked), when you break it and bring out what is in it. From its inverted form also comes: "qafasat al-shay'," when you take something out of the possession of its owner by usurpation. Then it was used for departing from the intended course and stripping away from the truth.

Ru'ba said:

"Deviating from their intended course, veering aside."

[[The explanation of this witness was given earlier, in the first volume, page 119; refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector.)]]

Ibn Mas'ud recited "fatabayyanu" (so verify) instead of "fatathabbatu." Tathabbut (verification) and tabayyun (clarification) are close in meaning; both mean seeking firmness, clarity, and knowing the facts. Since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and those with him held a rank that no one would dare to tell them a lie, and such a mistake as al-Walid's would happen only rarely, it was said that the conditional "in" (if) with the particle of doubt is used here. [Note: the text says "قيل: إن جاءكم بحرف الشك" which is Zamakhshari's statement that the conditional particle "in" is used, which carries a sense of doubt.] It also implies that the believers should be in this state, so that a wrongdoer will not be tempted to address them with a false word.

"Lest you harm a people in ignorance" (an tusibu qawman bijahalah): the phrase "an tusibu" is an object of purpose, meaning: out of aversion to harming a people in ignorance. "In ignorance" is a circumstantial phrase (hal), like His saying, ﴿And Allah turned back those who disbelieved in their rage﴾ [Q 33:25]. That is, not knowing the reality of the matter or the true nature of the story. The word "isbah" here means "becoming."

Regret (nadam) is a kind of grief. It is that you grieve over what has happened from you, wishing it had not happened. It is a grief that accompanies a person as a constant, lasting companion. Because every time the one who regrets remembers what he regrets, it returns to him. It comes from "nadam," which is the constant companionship of a drinking partner and his enduring company. From its inverted forms comes "adman al-amr" (he persisted in the matter), "adamahu" (he made it constant). And "madan bil-makan" means he stayed in the place. From it comes "al-madinah" (the city). You will find that people make worry a companion, a confidant, a boon-companion, a bedfellow, and describe it as never leaving its companion.

The clause introduced by "law" (if only / had it not been that) cannot be a new, independent statement, because that would lead to a discordance in the structure of the speech. [[Mahmud said: "The clause introduced by 'law' cannot be independent, because that would lead to a discordance in the structure of the speech..." Ahmad said: Among the flaws of the Mu'tazilah is their vilification of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, and their hesitation to rule on the punishment of his killers. To this belief, which they hold without hesitation, is added what al-Zamakhshari brings up in this passage of stories about Uthman's appointing his brother al-Walid, who committed that monstrous act, in place of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, one of the Companions, and what he alludes to, that some Companions would commit faults. Among them was their demanding that the Prophet ﷺ follow their opinions, among which was the acceptance of al-Walid's report about the attack on the Banu al-Mustaliq. If you combine this brief passage with what you know of his creed, what is clear about the state of al-Zamakhshari is something I cannot bring myself to state openly. He did not state it openly, and we have adopted with him the path of fairness and the way of retribution: text for text, allusion for allusion. So we ask Allah, the Mighty, after blessing His Prophet Muhammad, the seal of the prophets, to be pleased with all his Companions, and with us through them. Amin.]] Rather, it is connected to what came before it, as a circumstantial clause (hal) from one of the two pronouns in "fikum" (among you): either the hidden nominative pronoun or the apparent genitive pronoun. Both are sound opinions. The meaning is: "Among you is the Messenger of Allah in a state that you must change," or "You are in a state that you must change, namely that you seek from him to act in events according to what you think, and to consider right the conduct of one who obeys another, following him in his opinion and imitating his example." If he did that, "you would have been in distress," that is, you would have fallen into distress and ruin. It is said: "Fulan ya'attu fulanan," meaning he seeks what leads the other to ruin. And "a'natal 'azm" means the bone was broken after being set.

This indicates that some believers adorned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the idea of attacking the Banu al-Mustaliq and accepting al-Walid's statement. It also indicates that similar faults used to occur among them, and some of them would hold back, and their earnestness in piety would restrain them from daring to do so. These are the ones whom He excepted with His saying, ﴿But Allah has made faith beloved to you﴾ [Q 49:7], meaning: beloved to some of you. But He omitted mention of the some, because the description of them is distinct from the description of others. This is one of the Qur'an's concise expressions and subtle allusions, which only the elite notice. It is reported from some exegetes: they are those whose hearts Allah has tested for piety.

His saying, ﴿Those are the rightly guided﴾ [Q 49:7], is addressed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, meaning: those excepted are the rightly guided, confirming what you said. If you ask: what is the benefit of placing the predicate of "inna" (indeed) before its subject? I say: the purpose is to rebuke some believers for what Allah found reprehensible among them, namely making the opinion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ follow their opinions. So it was necessary to place it first, since the aim falls upon it.

If you ask: why was it said ﴿yuti'ukum﴾ (obeys you) and not "ata'akum" (obeyed you)? I say: to indicate that in their wish, his action should continue according to what they think right, and that whenever an opinion occurred to them about a matter, it would be acted upon. The evidence is His saying, ﴿in many matters﴾ [Q 49:7], like your saying: "Fulan entertains guests and protects the sanctity of women." You mean: this is something he is accustomed to and it is constantly found in him.

If you ask: how is "lakinna" (but) used when its conditions are absent, namely that what follows contradicts what precedes, in negation and affirmation? I say: it is absent in form but present in meaning, because those to whom faith was made beloved have a description different from the description of those previously mentioned. So "lakinna" falls at the very point of its function as a corrective contrast. The meaning of Allah making faith beloved and making disbelief hateful is kindness, support, and enabling with success. [[He resumed his speech: "The meaning of Allah making beloved and making hateful is kindness and support by enabling with success..." Ahmad said: He stammered, while the truth is clear; he went astray, while the path is straight. He measured the creation by the One True God, and made their actions belong to them, whether faith or disbelief, good or evil, deluded by a state he believed to be consistent in witnessed reality: that a person is not praised for another's action. He measured the unseen by the seen arbitrarily, and was led astray by following his desire into a self-conceit. This drove him, indeed emboldened him, to interpret the verse and nullify what I mentioned about attributing the making beloved of faith to Allah, the Exalted, in its literal sense. He made it metaphorical, because he believes that if it remained on its apparent meaning, the creation of faith would be attributed to Allah, and the servant would be praised for what is not his own action. For him this is impossible, so he subjected the verse to his corrupt opinion. When rational proofs for Oneness are presented to him, and textual proofs that there is no creator but Allah, the creator of all things, and he is asked to keep the verse on its apparent meaning, supported by reason and tradition, he clings to the aforementioned ropes in his interpretation, by arbitrary analogy of the unseen to the seen. This is a means to distort the Book of Allah, which falsehood cannot approach from before it or behind it. What we believe, may Allah keep us firm upon the truth, is that Allah, the Exalted, grants, praises, gives, and bestows favour. There is no existent except Allah and His attributes and actions. But He, the Exalted, made some of His actions a locus for others, so He named the locus "the doer" and the attribute "the act." This is the tawhid from which the believer has no escape or refuge. And I must argue with him and say: Tell me about Allah's praise of His prophets and messengers, by which is meant His choosing them for His preference. Is it through something acquired or through something not acquired? He cannot but say that He praised them for what they did not acquire, but rather what He gave them and they received. If he moves to the other side, which is the claim that He praised them for something they acquired, such as a messengership or prophethood, he has left the community of the faith and deviated from the people of the qibla. This brief statement is sufficient, Allah willing.]] Its method is metonymy, as previously explained. Every person of intellect and insight, whose mind reflects, does not fail to understand that a man is not praised for what is not his action. To interpret the verse literally leads to praising them for Allah's action, and Allah has negated this from those about whom He revealed, ﴿And they love to be praised for what they have not done﴾ [Q 3:188].

If you say: the Arabs praise beauty and good looks, and that is an action of Allah, and it is an acceptable praise among people, not rejected. I say: what permitted this for them is that they saw good appearance and attractiveness of countenance, which in general reveal a pleasing inner character and praiseworthy morals. For this reason they said, "The best of the ugly is the face." So they did not make it an attribute of praise in itself, but as an indication of something else. Moreover, some of the verifying scholars of reliable transmission and the scholars of meanings rejected the soundness of this and the error of the one who praises by it. They restricted praise to description by the mothers of goodness: eloquence, bravery, justice, and chastity, and what branches from them and returns to them. They considered describing someone by beauty, wealth, abundance of grandchildren and supporters, and other things in which a person has no action, to be an error and a deviation from reason.

Al-kufr (disbelief) means covering over the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, and concealing them by denial. Al-fusuq (wrongdoing) means departing from the intention of faith and its path by committing major sins. Al-'isyan (disobedience) means refusing to submit and to proceed with what the Lawgiver commanded. "Al-'irq al-'asi" (the disobedient vein) means the one that keeps flowing. "I'tasat al-nawah" means the date-stone became hard. Al-rushd (rightness) means steadfastness upon the path of truth with firmness in it, from "al-rashadah," which is a rock. Abu al-Wazi' said: every rock is a rashadah. He recited:

"And a tent-peg, not hung with a rope, and branded hearths, scorched by the light from solid rocks."

[[The apparent meaning is that the poet describes the dwellings as having nothing left in them except the tent-peg fastened with a rope, and the hearthstones whose color was changed by fire. "Wash" and "tawshim" mean changing the color, that is, they were burnt by their light, meaning their heat. "From solid rocks" explains what they are. "Al-summ" is the plural of "samma'," meaning hard. "Al-rashad" means rock, its singular is "rashadah." It was also said: he describes mounts as naturally disposed to work, not needing a bridle, and that their trace of travel is strong, to the extent that sparks appear from the intensity of their light footfall on the hard rock.]]

"Fadlan" (as a favour) is an object of purpose, or a verbal noun not from its own verb. [[Zamakhshari parsed "fadlan" in the verse as an object of purpose, dependent on his saying "al-rashidun" (the rightly guided)... Ahmad said: He raised the difficulty after establishing that rightness is not an act of Allah, the Exalted, but rather their own act in reality, according to his belief. We, however, have built upon what we explained: that rightness is one of the acts and creations of Allah. So the condition for the object of purpose has been met, namely the unity of the agent of the two verbs. Moreover, the difficulty arises explicitly on our view, though not in the way Zamakhshari stated it. Rather, Allah, the Exalted, addressed His creation in their familiar language, and something they are accustomed to is that the agent is the one to whom the act is attributed, whether that is literal or metaphorical, so that "the foam is the agent," "the wall collapsed," and such are like that. Rightness has been attributed to them according to the manner in which they are the agents, even if the attribution is metaphorical from the viewpoint of belief. Once this is established as being the case, you have two ways of answering it: either Zamakhshari's answer, or what is possible from it and clearer, which is that rightness here implies being rightly guided, since it is its counterpart, because Allah guided them and so they became rightly guided. Then the agent is unified in the manner of the grammatical discipline that agrees with reality. This is the reverse of His saying, ﴿He shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope﴾ [Q 13:12], where the difficulty exactly applies, since fear and hope are their acts, meaning attributed to them in the manner that they are the ones who fear and hope, while the first verb belongs to Allah, since He shows them that. The answer to it is that they are the ones acted upon in the meaning of the agents, through the implication of the reciprocal verb, because when He shows them, they have seen. This answer was given earlier in its place, so I have corrected the statement here by taking the object as the agent, and the reverse of that is the verse of al-Hujurat, where the statement is corrected by taking the agent as the object. This is one of the subtleties of Arabic, so reflect on it. And Allah is the Granter of success.]] If you ask: from where did it become permissible for it to be an object of purpose, when rightness is the act of the people and favour is the act of Allah, the Exalted, and the condition is that the agent be one? I say: since rightness became an expression for making beloved, making attractive, and making hateful, attributed to His name, may His names be sanctified, rightness became as if it were His act. So it is permissible for it to be governed by that, or not governed by "al-rashidun," but governed by the verb attributed to the name of Allah, the Exalted, and the sentence "those are the rightly guided" is a parenthetical insertion. Or it is governed by a suppressed verb, as if it were said: "That occurred," or "That was a favour from Allah." As for its being a verbal noun not from its own verb, it is because it is placed in the position of "rushd" (rightness), since their rightness is a favour from Allah, as they were enabled in it. And favour and bounty are in the sense of bestowing and conferring.

﴿And Allah is Knowing﴾ of the conditions of the believers and the distinctions and differences among them, ﴿Wise﴾ when He bestows favour and blessing by enabling success upon the most excellent of them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 49, verse 9:

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by a gathering of some of the Ansar while he was riding a donkey, and the donkey urinated. ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy covered his nose and said: "Let go of your donkey, for its stench has harmed us." ʿAbdullah ibn Rawahah said: "By Allah, the urine of his donkey is more fragrant than your musk." [[I have not seen it from Ibn ʿAbbas. It is in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Anas, and in it: "We were told that it was revealed: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight...﴾ to the end of the verse," without the mention of the donkey's urine. And his saying "By Allah, the urine of his donkey is more fragrant than your musk" is not in it, nor is "The Prophet (ﷺ) went on, and then the verse was revealed."]] And it is also narrated: "His donkey is better than you, and the urine of his donkey is more fragrant than your musk." [[I have not seen it in this form. The hadith of Anas in the two Sahihs says: "By Allah, the donkey of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has a more fragrant smell than you."]] The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went on, and the dispute between them lengthened until they came to blows and grappled with each other. Their two peoples, the Aws and the Khazraj, came, and they fought with sticks; it is said they also fought with their hands, sandals and palm fronds. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned to them and reconciled between them, and the verse was revealed.

It is narrated from Muqatil that he recited it to them, and they reconciled.

Al-baghy (transgression, from the root meaning to seek to overpower): it means oppression, injustice, and refusal to make peace. Al-fayʾ (returning): it means to return, and it has been applied to shade and to spoils of war, because shade returns after the sun has moved on, and ghanimah (spoils) is that which returns from the wealth of the disbelievers to the Muslims.

It is narrated from Abu ʿAmr that he read ﴿حَتَّىٰ تَفِي﴾ without hamzah. Its basis is that Abu ʿAmr eased the first of the two meeting hamzahs, so that this slight change escaped the narrator, and he thought that it had been dropped. [[His saying "that slight change" (تلك الخلسة): in al-Sihah: "I snatched the thing and seized it, when I took it away; and the noun is khilsah, with a dammah." (ʿ)]]

If you say: What is the reason for His saying ﴿اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ when the analogical form would be ﴿اقْتَتَلَتَا﴾, as Ibn Abi ʿAblah read? Or ﴿اقْتَتَلَا﴾, as ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read, in accordance with the interpretation of "the two groups" or "the two parties"? I say: It is one of the cases where the verb is taken according to meaning rather than according to the wording, because al-ṭāʾifatān (the two groups) is in meaning "people" and "folk."

In the reading of ʿAbdullah: ﴿حَتَّىٰ يَفِيئُوا إِلَىٰ أَمْرِ اللَّهِ ۚ فَإِنْ فَاءُوا فَخُذُوا بَيْنَهُمَا بِالْقِسْطِ﴾.

The ruling on the transgressing group: it is obligatory to fight it for as long as it fights. It is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar: "I have felt nothing in my soul as much as I felt about this verse: that I did not fight this transgressing group, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic commanded me." He said this after he had withdrawn (from the fighting). So if they cease and withdraw their hands from war, they are left alone; and if they turn away, one acts in accordance with what has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "O son of Umm ʿAbd, do you know how Allah has ruled concerning those who transgress within this community?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Do not finish off its wounded, do not kill its captives, do not pursue its fugitive, and do not divide its spoils." [[Recorded by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak, al-Bazzar, al-Harith, and Ibn ʿAdi, from the narration of Kawthar ibn Hakim al-Naqi, from Nafiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar. Kawthar is abandoned (matruk); Ahmad said of him: "His hadiths are falsehoods."]]

The two groups of Muslims in their fighting cannot be outside one of the following: either they fight out of transgression on both sides, and then what is obligatory is that one should intervene between them with what restores harmony and produces reconciliation and peace. If they do not withdraw and do not make peace, and they persist in transgression, then one proceeds to fight both of them. Or the fighting between them flares up because of a doubt that has entered upon them, while each of them regards itself as being in the right. Then what is obligatory is to remove the doubt with clear proofs and decisive evidence, and to make them aware of the paths of truth. If they plunge into obstinate dispute and do not act in accordance with what they have been guided to and advised to follow of the truth after its clarity to them, then they have joined the two transgressing groups. Or one of them is the transgressor against the other, and then what is obligatory is to fight the transgressing group until it desists and repents. If it does so, one reconciles between them and the group that was wronged with justice and fairness. There are details in this: if the transgressing group is small in number, with no protection, it is liable for what it has done after it returns. If it is large, with strength and power, it is not held liable, except according to Muhammad ibn al-Hasan (may Allah have mercy on him), for he used to give the legal opinion that liability falls on it when it returns. As for before gathering and mobilising, or when they disperse when the war lays down its burdens, then what it has committed it is liable for according to all. So the meaning of reconciliation with justice in His saying ﴿فَأَصْلِحُوا بَيْنَهُمَا بِالْعَدْلِ﴾ according to the school of Muhammad is clear and fits the wording of the revelation. According to the view of others, it is understood as applying to the case where the group is small in number. As for what they mention, that the aim is the extinguishing of rancour and the removal of hatreds without liability for offences, it is not a fitting match for what was commanded of acts of justice and maintaining fairness.

If you say: Why did He link justice to the second reconciliation and not the first? I say: Because what is meant by fighting at the beginning of the verse is that the two groups fight while both are transgressing, or both are riding on a doubt, and whichever of them it is, what the Muslims must do regarding them is to reconcile between them, calm the masses (al-dahmaʾ, meaning the multitude) by showing the truth, with comforting admonitions, and by removing doubt, unless they persist. Then fighting becomes obligatory. As for liability, it does not apply in this case. It is not so if one of them transgresses, for then liability applies in both of the cases mentioned. ﴿وَأَقْسِطُوا﴾ is a command to act with justice in a general way, after it was commanded in reconciling between them. The discussion of it is like the discussion of the command to fear Allah following the prohibition of putting oneself forward before Him.

Al-qist, with a fatha, is injustice, from the root al-qist, which is a crookedness in the legs. [[His saying "which is a crookedness in the legs": in al-Sihah: al-qist (with fatha on the qaf, and the sukun ... ) is a splaying in the legs of an animal, and that is a defect, because bending and straightening are preferred in them.(ʿ)]] A "qasit" wood means dry. And "the winds made it qasit" (aqsatahu al-riyah) means they dried it. As for qist in the sense of justice, its verb is aqsaṭa, and the hamzah in it is for negation, meaning: he removed qist, which is injustice.

This is a statement of what has been made binding on those who take up the task of reconciling believers who have fallen into conflict, and an explanation that faith has tied its people together by a close cause and an adhesive kinship. Whatever does not add to brotherhood and does not stand out above it does not diminish it, nor fall short of its goal. Moreover, the custom of people is that when such a dispute arises between two brothers of the same parentage, those nearby must hasten to lift it and remove it, mounting the difficult and the easy alike in pursuit of reconciliation, and sending emissaries (safara') between them (the plural of safir, meaning the messenger and the one who reconciles between people), until what has become weak in harmony meets someone who mends it, and what has become dry in connection meets someone who moistens it. Brotherhood in religion is more deserving of this, and of something stronger than it.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "A Muslim is the brother of a Muslim: he does not wrong him, nor forsake him, nor belittle him, nor exalt himself over him in building so as to block the wind from him without his permission, nor harm him with the steam of his cooking pot." Then he said, "Remember, and few of you will remember." (Al-Tha'labi related it from the narration of Isma'il ibn Rafi', from Sa'id, from Abu Hurayra, with the same wording, and added: "...nor harm him with the steam of his cooking pot unless he ladles some out for him. Nor should they buy fruit for their children and then take it out to the children of their neighbour without feeding them from it." I say: its chain is weak, but the beginning of the hadith is in the Two Sahihs from another route from Abu Hurayra, and it will come at the end of the tafsir of Surat al-Waqi'a.)

If you ask: why is the dual singled out for mention rather than the plural? I answer: because the least number among whom discord occurs is two. So when reconciliation is required between the least, it is all the more required among the greater, since corruption in the discord of a group is greater than in the discord of two. It was also said: the intended "two brothers" are the Aws and the Khazraj. It was read: "between your brothers" (ikhwatikum) and "your fellow-brothers" (ikhwanikum). The meaning: the believers are nothing but brothers, and they are pure and unmixed in this; the doubts of foreignness have been removed from them, and the gentleness of their state in mingling and unity refuses that they proceed to what gives rise to severance. So they hasten to cut off whatever of that occurs, if it occurs, and to put an end to it. "And fear God" — for if you do so, piety will not move you except toward connection and harmony, and hastening to remove whatever has been neglected of it. And when you do that, the arrival of God's mercy to you and the enveloping of His compassion over you is worthy that you base your hope upon it.

The people (al-qawm) refers specifically to men, because they are the ones in charge of women's affairs. God the Exalted said: ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ [4:34]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Women are meat on a wadm (a piece of wood or other material placed under meat to keep it off the ground) [[Its meaning: the wadm is what is placed beneath the meat, of wood or something else, to protect it from the ground. Reported by al-Sihah.]] except what is defended," and those who defend are men. Qawm is in origin the plural of qa'im (one standing), like sawwam and zawwar as plurals of sa'im (one fasting) and za'ir (one visiting). Or it is a naming by the verbal noun. From some Arabs: "When you eat food, you love sleep and hate qawm," meaning qiyam (standing). That qawm is restricted to men is clear in the verse and in the verse of Zuhayr:

*I do not know, and I suppose I will soon know: are they the people of Hisn, or women?*
*If the women are veiled, then every chaste woman deserves to be guided [to her husband].*

Zuhayr is satirizing Hisn ibn Hudhayfah al-Fazari. Qawm means men only, so much so that it has been said it is the plural of qa'im, like sawwam and zawwar for sa'im and za'ir. It has also been said that it is originally a verbal noun, and the hamza is for seeking specification, but the matter is among the obscurities of the knowers. Nisa' (women) is coordinated with qawm, and is either a predicate after "Al Hisn," or a predicate of an omitted subject, and the coordination is one of sentences. It is also possible that the hamza is for equalization, like the one that occurs after sawa'. It is as if he said: "I do not care which of them they are, whether men or women," in which case it is definitely coordination of sentences for the sake of equalization. But the context supports the first reading. In the line there is an interruption between sawfa and what it governs, with the verb placed at the object, and also an interruption between "ma adri" and the interrogative by the clause of deferment, because adri requires two objects and the clause "aqawm" fills their place. Observe how it occurred to him to deny knowledge of the state of the family, then before completing that, it occurred to him to affirm that he would soon know, then before completing that, he said that gaining knowledge in the future is by way of imagination and supposition. So he related the state of the soul as it hesitates over the matter. How refined the Arabs were in relating a state with the most eloquent speech. It is also narrated as "lasta" in place of "sawfa," but there is something to consider in that. The subject of takun is the pronoun of qawm, nisa' is its predicate, and mukhabba'at is a circumstantial clause, meaning: if they (the women) are chaste, then it is right for them to guide [their husbands]. The guiding of a woman to her husband, and making her guide him, is the same meaning.

As for their saying regarding the people of Pharaoh and the people of 'Ad: that they are males and females, the word qawm does not thereby include both groups. Rather, the intent is to mention the males and omit mentioning the females, because they are followers of their men. The indefiniteness of "qawm" and "nisa'" allows two meanings: that it refers to "some believers and some believing women," and that it is intended to convey generality, so that each group is forbidden from mockery. [[Mahmud said: "He did not say: 'Some believers should not mock some believing women...'" Ahmad said: If he had used the definite form and said: "Believers should not mock one another," each group would be forbidden by necessity of the comprehensiveness of the prohibition. But al-Zamakhshari raised this point, and he intended that indefiniteness has the benefit that each group is forbidden in detail, and that the prohibition addresses each group individually. With the definite form, the prohibition is achieved but not in detail, only in generality. The detailed prohibition is more eloquent and more forceful.]] He did not say "a man from a man" nor "a woman from a woman" in the singular, [[He resumed his words. He said: "He did not say a man from a man nor a woman from a woman, to indicate..." Ahmad said: It is in the utmost beauty, nothing can be added to it.]] to indicate that more than one of their men and more than one of their women engage in mockery, and to express horror at the state they were in. Also, the scene of a mocker is rarely free of someone who is amused and laughs at his words, and does not carry out the prohibition and disapproval required of him. So he becomes a partner of the mocker and a follower in bearing the burden. Likewise everyone whose hearing it reaches, who finds it pleasing and laughs at it. Thus that leads, even if one person initiated it, to the multiplication of mockery and the transformation of an individual into a group and a people. God the Exalted's words ﴿Perhaps they are better than them﴾ [49:11] are a new sentence which came as an answer to one who asks about the cause of the prohibition that was revealed. [[Mahmud said: "His words 'perhaps they are better than them' are an answer to one who asks about the cause of the prohibition..." Ahmad said: This is of the first class.]] Otherwise, it should have been connected to what precedes it with a fa' (so). The meaning is that everyone must believe that the one being mocked may be better in God's sight than the mocker, because people perceive only outward conditions and have no knowledge of hidden matters. What weighs in God's sight is only the sincerity of hearts and the piety of souls, and people have no access to that. So no one should dare to mock someone whose appearance looks down upon him, when he sees him in shabby condition, or having a defect in his body, or lacking eloquence in conversation. For perhaps he is more sincere in heart and more pious in soul than one who is the opposite of his description. Thus he wrongs himself by belittling one whom God has honored, and by disparaging one whom God has exalted. The early generation reached such extremes in guarding and protecting themselves from this that 'Amr ibn Sharahil said: "If I saw a man suckling a she-goat and I laughed at him, I would fear I might do the same thing he did." [[I did not find it from him, but in Ibn Abi Shaybah from Abu Musa there is something similar as his own statement.]] And 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "Calamity is entrusted to speech. If I mocked a dog, I would fear that I would be transformed into a dog." [[Reported by Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Adab al-Mufrad from the narration of Ibrahim from Ibn Mas'ud in this way.]] In the reading of 'Abd Allah: ﴿'Asu an yakunu...﴾ and ﴿'Asin an yakunna...﴾ [masculine and feminine forms]. So 'asa in this reading has a predicate, like the one in His words ﴿Then would you perhaps...﴾ [47:22], and in the first reading which has no predicate, like His words ﴿And it may be that you dislike something﴾ [2:216]. Al-lamz is slandering and striking with the tongue.

It was also read as "wa la talmizu" with a damma. The meaning: specifically, O believers, prohibit yourselves from disparaging yourselves and slandering them, and there is no harm in your criticizing others who do not follow your religion or conduct themselves by your way. In a hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Mention the wicked person for what he has done, so that people may be wary of him." [[Reported by Abu Ya'la, al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in al-Nawadir in the sixty-eighth section, al-'Uqayli, Ibn 'Adi and Ibn Hibban, all from the narration of al-Jarud ibn Yazid from Bahz ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather, as a marfu' report: "Do you refrain from mentioning the wicked? Mention him for what is in him, so that people may be wary of him." They agreed that al-Jarud is not trustworthy, and al-Daraqutni said: "It is a fabrication of al-Jarud, then a group stole it from him, among them 'Amr ibn al-Azhar, and Sulayman ibn 'Isa, from al-Thawri, from Bahz, and Sulayman, and 'Amr, thus it is clear." It was also narrated by al-'Ala' ibn Bashir from Ibn 'Uyaynah from Bahz. Al-Daraqutni said: Ibn 'Uyaynah did not hear from Bahz, and he changed the wording and said: "There is no backbiting for a wicked person." This was cited by al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab from al-Hakim with his chain to al-'Ala'. Al-Hakim said: This is not authentic and not reliable. Ibn Tahir said: It was also narrated from Ma'mar from Bahz, reported by 'Abd al-Wahhab, brother of 'Abd al-Razzaq, but 'Abd al-Wahhab is a liar. It was also reported by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, who said: No one narrated it from Ma'mar except him. He said: There is another chain from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, narrated by Yusuf ibn Aban: al-Abrad ibn Hatim informed us, Manhal al-Sarraj informed me, from 'Umar.]] Al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him), in mentioning al-Hajjaj, said: "He brought out to us short fingers, which seldom had their reins stained in the cause of God." Then he began to pat some of his hair and say: "O Abu Sa'id, O Abu Sa'id." And when he died, he said: "O God, You have made him die, so cut off his tradition, for he came to us as a squint-eyed, weak-eyed man [[His words 'akhayfash a'aymash': in the Sihah, al-khafash is smallness in the eye and weakness of sight by nature, and the man is akhfash. Also, al-'amash in the eye is weakness of vision with flowing of tears, and the man is a'mash. Akhayfash and a'ayamash are diminutives of akhfash and a'mash.]] who swaggered in his walk and climbed the pulpit until the prayer passed him by, fearing neither God nor people." Above him was God, and beneath him were a hundred thousand or more, and no one said to him: "The prayer, O man! The prayer, O man!" Far from that, the sword and the whip. It was also said: its meaning is: do not find fault with one another, because believers are like one soul, so when a believer finds fault with a believer, it is as though he found fault with himself. It was also said: its meaning is: do not do what you would be slandered for, because whoever does what deserves slander has in reality slandered himself.

Tanabuz bil-alqab (mutual nicknaming with titles): calling one another by them. It is a reciprocal form from nabazahu, and the Banu so-and-so mutually call one another by them, and it is said: al-nabz and al-nabz (both forms) mean the bad title. The forbidden naming is that which the one called dislikes, because it is a belittling of him, a blame, and a disgrace. As for what he loves, which adorns him and makes him famous, there is no harm in it. It was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Among the rights of a believer over his brother is that he call him by the name he likes best." [[I have not found it this way. Al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Shu'ab, in the sixty-first section, from 'Uthman ibn Talhah al-Hajabi, raising it: "Three things purify the love of your brother: you greet him when you meet him, you make room for him in the gathering, and you call him by the name he likes best." In its chain is Musa ibn 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr, who is weak. Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani narrated from the hadith of Dhayyal ibn 'Ubayd ibn Hanzalah: my grandfather Hanzalah ibn Jadhim told me: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) liked that a man be called by the name he liked best."]] For this reason, kunyah (calling by a patronymic) is from the Sunnah and good manners.

'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Spread cauterization, for it is a reminder." Abu Bakr was given the titles al-'Atiq and al-Siddiq, 'Umar was given al-Faruq, Hamzah was given Asad Allah (Lion of God), and Khalid was given Sayf Allah (Sword of God). Few famous people, in the pre-Islamic period or in Islam, are without a title. Such good titles have continued among all nations, Arab and non-Arab, in their speech and writing without objection. It was reported from al-Dahhak that some of the Banu Tamim mocked Bilal, Khabbab, 'Ammar, Suhayb, Abu Dharr, and Salim the client of Hudhayfah, and so this was revealed. And from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her): she used to mock Zaynab bint Khuzaymah al-Hilaliyyah, who was short. From Ibn 'Abbas: Umm Salamah tied her waistband with a sabibah [[His words 'hiqwayha bi-sabibah': in the Sihah, al-sabb is a piece of linen cloth, and al-sabibah is similar to it.]] and let its end trail behind her, and she used to drag it. So 'A'ishah said to Hafsah: "Look at what she drags behind her, as if it were a dog's tongue." And from Anas: the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reproached Umm Salamah for being short.

From 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: Safiyyah bint Huyayy came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "The women taunt me, saying: 'O Jewess, daughter of two Jews!'" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her: "Why did you not say: 'My father is Harun, my uncle is Musa, and my husband is Muhammad'?" [[Al-Tha'labi mentioned it from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, without a chain. In al-Tirmidhi, from the narration of Hashim ibn Sa'id al-Kufi: Kinanah told us, Safiyyah bint Huyayy told us: "I entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and I had received word of some talk from 'A'ishah and Hafsah. I mentioned that to him, and he said: 'Why did you not say: "How could they be better than me, when my husband is Muhammad (ﷺ), my father is Harun, and my uncle is Musa (peace be upon them)?"'" The word that reached her was that they said: "We are more honored by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) than she is, and better than her: we are his wives and the daughters of his uncle." He said: It is strange, and its chain is not that strong. Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban, Ahmad and al-Tabarani narrated from the narration of Ma'mar from Thabit from Anas: "It reached Safiyyah that Hafsah said: 'Daughter of a Jew.' So she wept..." and mentioned its meaning.]] It is also narrated that it was revealed about Thabit ibn Qays, who was hard of hearing, and they used to make room for him in the gathering of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so he could hear. One day he came saying: "Make room for me," until he reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said to a man: "Move over!" The man did not move, so he said: "Who is this?" The man said: "I am so-and-so." He said: "No, you are the son of such-and-such a woman," meaning: he was reproached for her in the pre-Islamic period. The man was embarrassed, and so this was revealed. Thabit said: "I will never boast over anyone about lineage after this, ever." [[Al-Tha'labi mentioned it, and whoever followed him, from Ibn 'Abbas, without a chain.]] Al-ism (the name) here means the mention, from their saying: "His name flew among the people for generosity or for baseness," just as one says: "his praise and his reputation flew." Its reality is: what rose from his mention and was elevated among people. Do you not see their saying: "He raised his mention"? It is as if it were said: "Wretched is the elevated mention for the believers" [[Mahmud said: "Al-ism here is the mention, from their saying: 'His name flew among the people for generosity.' It is as if he said: 'Wretched is the elevated mention for the believers...'" Ahmad said: The closest of the three ways to fit the rule of the people of the Sunnah, and the best of them, is the first, but after diverting the blame to fisq itself, which is correct because the ism is the musamma (named thing). But al-Zamakhshari could not do that: he deviated toward a principle that the blame is diverted to the elevation of the mention of wickedness from a believer, out of fear that ism means naming, and there is no doubt that diverting the blame to fisq itself is better. As for the second way, he brought it in to complete his taking of ism as naming explicitly. As for the third, it is to complete his claim that the wicked person is not a believer, and both principles oppose the Sunnah, so beware of them. And God is the Granter of success. God has revealed to me His purposes, such that no word that deviates to the faction of innovation is turned into anything except that the truth overtakes it and speaks to it. Praise be to God.]] on account of committing these sins [[His words 'hadhihi al-jara'ir': plural of jarirah, which is a crime. Reported by al-Sihah.]] that they be mentioned with wickedness. And in His words ﴿after faith﴾ [49:11] there are three aspects. The first is the condemnation of combining faith with wickedness, which faith rejects and forbids, as you say: "Wretched is the affair after maturity, the youthful folly" [[His words 'ba'da al-kabrah al-sabwah': al-kabrah with a fatha is the name for old age, and al-sabwah is inclination toward ignorance and youthful folly. Reported by al-Sihah.]]. The second: that in their insults to a Jew who had become Muslim, they would say: "O Jew! O wicked one!" and so they were forbidden from this, and it was said to them: "Wretched is the mention that you mention a man with wickedness and Judaism after his faith." On this interpretation, the sentence is connected to the prohibition against nicknames. The third: that it is taken as referring to one who commits wickedness without being a believer, just as you say to one who switches from trade to farming: "Wretched is the profession of farming after trade."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 49, verse 12:

It is said: "jannabahu al-sharr" (he kept evil far from him) when he removed it from himself. Its underlying sense is: he placed it on a side away from him, so it is transitive to two objects.

God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And keep me and my sons far from worshipping idols﴾ [Qur'an 14:35]. Then, in its reflexive form, it is said: "ijtanaba al-sharr" (he avoided evil), so the reflexive form drops one object. The thing one is commanded to avoid is some of the suspicion, and that part is described as being many: do you not see His saying: ﴿Indeed, some suspicion is sin﴾?

If you say: what is the distinction between the word "kathiran" (much), where it came indefinite, and where it would have come definite? I say: its coming indefinite conveys the meaning of "partiality" (some of), and indeed among suspicions there is that which must be avoided without its being specified or determined, so that no one dares to entertain any suspicion except after reflection and deliberation, and distinguishing between its truth and its falsehood by a clear indication, while sensing piety and caution. Had it been definite, the command to avoid suspicion would have been tied to what is abundant of it rather than what is little, and it would have been necessary that every suspicion described as abundant be avoided, while what is described as little be permitted in entertaining it. What distinguishes the suspicions that must be avoided from others is this: every suspicion for which no sound indication and apparent cause is known is forbidden and must be avoided. This applies when the person suspected is one who has been seen to be concealing (his faults) and righteous, and who is trusted outwardly in trustworthiness; then suspecting him of corruption and treachery is forbidden, unlike one whom people know for engaging in doubtful matters and openly committing vile deeds.

From the Prophet ﷺ:

"Indeed God, the Exalted, has made forbidden from the Muslim his blood, his honour, and that one should think evil of him" [[Narrated by Ibn Majah, from the hadith of Ibn Umar with a chain containing weakness, and its wording is: "I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ circumambulating the Ka'bah and he was saying: How good you are and how good your fragrance is, how great you are and how great your sanctity is, and by the One in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, the sanctity of the believer is greater before God than your sanctity: his wealth, his blood, and that one should think of him only good." Ibn Abi Shaybah also related, by way of Mujalid from al-Sha'bi from Ibn Abbas, that the Prophet ﷺ looked at the Ka'bah and said: "How great you are and how great your sanctity is, and the Muslim has greater sanctity than you. God has made forbidden his blood, his wealth, his honour, and that one should think evil of him." al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related, by way of Mujahid from Ibn Abbas, something similar. In its chain is Hafs ibn Abd al-Rahman.]] And from al-Hasan: "We were in a time when suspecting people was forbidden, and you are today in a time of 'act and be silent, and suspect people as you wish.'"

And from him: "There is no sanctity for a wicked person." And from him: "If the wrongdoer displays his wrongdoing and tears away his veil, God will expose him; and if he conceals it, God does not expose him, perhaps he will repent." It has been related: "Whoever casts off the garment of shame, there is no backbiting for him" [[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab in the sixty-ninth (section), and al-Qada'i in Musnad al-Shihab, by way of a route related by Ibn al-Jarrah from Abu Sa'd al-Sa'idi from Anas, and its chain is weak. Ibn Adi related it from the narration of al-Rabi' ibn Badr from Aban from Anas, and its chain is weaker than the first.]].

"Al-ithm" (sin): the sin for which its doer deserves punishment. From it comes the name of its punishment: "al-athām," on the pattern of "al-nakāl," "al-adhāb," and "al-wabāl." He said:

"Indeed that intention (nawa) did to me a deed... may the nawa's consequences strike it before death"

[[The nawa: the intention of a traveller, whether near or far; it is feminine, and it is used as a collective noun of "niyyah," so it may be masculine. The meaning: indeed you did in this intention a wicked deed, so it is in the sense of "fi" (in). Then he invoked against it by saying: "may the nawa that harmed me strike its athām," i.e., the requital of that deed, or the requital of the nawa that deserves it. Sin may also be called "ithm" and "athām," by the figure of speech of naming the cause by its effect. He said "before death," i.e., before its death, so that he may be satisfied with it; as if he likened it to an enemy, then invoked against it.]]

The hamza in it is from the waw, as if it "yathimu" the deeds: that is, it breaks them by its nullifying them. It is also read "wa la tahassasu" with the ha', and the two meanings are close. It is said: "tajassasa al-amr" when one seeks it and investigates it; it is a form of "al-jass" (touching), just as "al-talammus" (groping) meaning seeking comes from "al-lams" (touching), because in touching there is seeking. It has come with the meaning of seeking in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed we touched the heaven﴾ [Qur'an 72:8]. And "al-tahassus" is coming to know through the senses (al-hiss); and because of their closeness, the human faculties are called "al-hawass" (the senses), with the ha' and the jim. The intended meaning is the prohibition of tracking the private faults and defects of the Muslims and probing into what they have concealed. From Mujahid: "Take what appears, and leave what God has concealed."

From the Prophet ﷺ: he delivered a sermon and raised his voice until he made the virgins in their chambers hear, and he said: "O assembly of those who have believed with their tongues while faith has not penetrated their hearts, do not follow the faults of the Muslims, for whoever follows the faults of the Muslims, God follows his fault until He disgraces him, even within his house" [[Narrated by al-Tabarani and al-Uqayli, and Ibn Adi, from the narration of Qudamah ibn Muhammad al-Ashja'i from Isma'il ibn Shabib al-Ta'ifi from Ibn Jurayj from Ata' from Ibn Abbas with this. On the same theme, from Ibn Umar, al-Tirmidhi related it, and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and its wording: "The Prophet ﷺ ascended the pulpit and called out in a loud voice: 'O assembly of those who have submitted with their tongues while faith has not reached their hearts, do not harm the Muslims, do not reproach them, and do not follow their faults, for whoever follows the fault of his Muslim brother, God follows his fault, and whoever God follows his fault, He will disgrace him, even within his riding-saddle.'" And from Abu Burdah in Abu Dawud, Ahmad, al-Tabarani, and Abu Ya'la; and from al-Bara' ibn Azib in Abu Ya'la and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab in the sixty-ninth, from the narration of Mus'ab ibn Salam from Abu Ishaq from al-Bara'. And from Thawban in Ahmad with the wording: "Do not harm the servants of God, do not reproach them, and do not seek their faults, for whoever seeks the fault of his Muslim brother, God seeks his fault until He disgraces him in his house." And from Buraydah in al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh, and its wording: "We prayed the noon prayer behind the Prophet ﷺ, and when he turned, he came to us angry and called out in a voice that made the virgins in the depths of their chambers hear," and he mentioned something similar.]]. And from Zayd ibn Wahb: we said to Ibn Mas'ud: "Do you want [to know about] al-Walid ibn Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, whose beard drips with wine?" Ibn Mas'ud said: "Indeed we have been forbidden from tajassus, so if something appears to us, we act upon it" [[Narrated by Abu Dawud, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd al-Razzaq, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab in the fifty-second, by various routes from al-A'mash from Zayd ibn Wahb who said: "Ibn Mas'ud was told: 'This is so-and-so, whose beard drips with wine.'" The wording of Abu Dawud and the others is similar. al-Hakim and al-Bazzar related it from the narration of Asbat from al-A'mash, and he said in it: "The Messenger of God ﷺ forbade us from tajassus." al-Bazzar said: Asbat alone related it. Ibn Abi Hatim said, from Abu Zur'ah, and al-Tirmidhi from al-Bukhari: Asbat erred in it.

The sound version, from the narration of Abu Mu'awiyah and others from al-A'mash, is: "Indeed God forbade us."]]. "Ghabahu" and "ightabahu" (to backbite): like "ghalahu" and "ightalahu" (to assassinate by stealth). "Al-ghibah" (backbiting) is from "al-ightiyab," like "al-ghilah" from "al-ightiyal" [[His saying "like al-ghilah from al-ightiyal": so it is in al-Sihah. In it one says: "qatalahu ghilatan," which is that he deceives him and takes him to a place and kills him there. (ʿA)]]:

It is the mention of evil in absence. The Messenger of God ﷺ was asked about backbiting and said: "It is that you mention your brother with what he dislikes. If it is in him, you have backbited him, and if it is not in him, you have slandered him" [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. And from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "Backbiting is the condiment of the dogs of people." ﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?﴾ This is a representation and depiction of what the backbiter inflicts upon the honour of the one he backbites, in the most hideous and foul form. In it are various intensifications: among them, the interrogative whose meaning is affirmation; among them, placing what is at the utmost of dislike as the object of "love"; among them, attributing the verb to "ahadukum" (one of you), and signalling that neither of the two individuals likes that; among them, that he did not restrict the representation of backbiting to eating human flesh, until he made the person a brother; among them, that he did not restrict it to eating the flesh of a brother until he made him dead. From Qatadah: "As you would dislike it, if you found a rotting carcass, to eat from it, so likewise dislike the flesh of your brother while he is alive." "Maytan" is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl) from "al-laḥm" (the flesh); it may also be accusative from "al-akh" (the brother). It is also read "maytan."

When God, Mighty and Majestic, established for them that none of them likes to eat the carcass of his brother, He followed that with His saying: ﴿So you have disliked it﴾; its meaning is: "fa-qad karihtumuhu" (so you have indeed disliked it), and it is settled. It contains the sense of a condition: that is, if this is established, then you have disliked it. It is the eloquent "fa" (fa al-fasīḥah), meaning: it is thereby verified—through the obligation of admission upon you, and that you cannot repel it or deny it, since human nature refuses that you deny it—your dislike of it and your revulsion from it; so let it likewise be verified that you dislike what is its counterpart, namely backbiting and defaming the honour of the Muslims. It is also read "fakarihtumuhu," meaning: you have been created with a disposition to dislike it. If you say: why was it not transitive with "ila" as in His saying, "wa karraha ilaykumu al-kufr" (and He made disbelief hateful to you)? And which of them is the analogy? I say: the analogy is that it is transitive by itself, because it is a verb with one object before the doubling of its middle radical; you say "karihtu al-shay'" (I disliked the thing), and when it is doubled, it requires an additional object. As for its being transitive with "ila," it is an interpretation and a treatment of "karaha" as if it were "baghada," because "baghada" is derived from "baghuda ilayhi al-shay'" (the thing became hateful to him), so he is "baghidun ilayhi" (hateful to him), just as you say "ḥubba ilayhi al-shay'" (the thing became beloved to him), so he is "ḥabībun ilayhi" (beloved to him).

The intensification in "al-tawwāb" (the Oft-Returning) is to indicate the multitude of those among His servants upon whom He turns in repentance, or because there is no sin committed by the sinner except that it is forgiven by repentance; or because He is eloquent in accepting repentance, placing its one who repents in the position of one who has never sinned at all, due to the vastness of His generosity.

The meaning: "And fear God by abandoning what you have been commanded to avoid and by regretting what has occurred from you of it, for if you fear God, God will accept your repentance and bestow upon you the reward of the pious who repent." From Ibn Abbas: Salman used to serve two men among the Companions and prepare their food for them. One day he slept through his task, so they sent him to the Messenger of God ﷺ to seek a condiment for them. Usamah was in charge of the food of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he said: "I have nothing." Salman informed them of that, whereupon they said: "If we had sent him to the well of Sumayhah, its water would have dried up." When they came to the Messenger of God ﷺ, he said to them: "What is this? I see the greenness of meat in your mouths." They said: "We have not eaten any meat." He said: "Indeed you have backbitten [people]" [[Thus it is related by al-Tha'labi, and Rabi'ah without chain or narrator. In al-Targhib of Abu al-Qasim al-Asbahani, by way of Hammad ibn Salamah from Thabit from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla something similar.]]. Then this verse was revealed.

from a male and a female: from Adam and Eve. It has also been said: We created each one of you from a father and a mother, so none of you is other than one who traces his lineage in the same way as the other, equal to equal. Therefore there is no basis for boasting or preferring oneself in lineage.

The *sha'b* (plural *shu'ub*; the first of the six levels of Arab social organization) is the first of the six tiers on which the Arabs were organized. They are: *sha'b*, *qabila* (tribe), *'imara* (clan), *batn* (subclan), *fakhdh* (lineage group), and *fasila* (household). The *sha'b* comprises the tribes, the tribe comprises the *'imarat*, the *'imara* comprises the *butun*, the *batn* comprises the *afkhadh*, and the *fakhdh* comprises the *fasa'il*. Khuzayma is a *sha'b*, Kinana is a *qabila*, Quraysh is an *'imara*, Qusayy is a *batn*, Hashim is a *fakhdh*, and al-'Abbas is a *fasila*. The *shu'ub* are so named because the tribes branched out (*tasha'aba*) from them.

It has been read as *li-tata'arafu* and *li-ta'arafu* (with assimilation), and *li-ta'rafu* and *li-tatarrafu*. The meaning of *li-ta'rafu* is: so that you may know how you are related to one another. The wisdom behind His arranging you into peoples and tribes is that some of you should know the lineage of others, so that no one claims descent from anyone other than his own fathers, not that you should boast of forefathers and grandfathers and insist on disparity and preference in lineages.

Then he explained the quality by which a person excels over another and gains honour and nobility with God Most High, saying: ﴿Indeed, the most honourable of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you﴾. It has also been read as *anna* (with a fatha), as if it were said: Why should one not boast of lineages? Then it is said: Because the most honourable of you in God's sight is the most righteous of you, not the one with the most distinguished lineage.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that on the day of the conquest of Mecca he circumambulated, praised God and extolled Him, then said: "Praise be to God who has removed from you the *'ubiyya* (arrogance) of the Jahiliyya and its pride. O people, people are of two kinds: a believer who is pious and noble before God, and a wicked wretch who is contemptible before God."

[The author's words "'ubiyyat al-jahiliyya": in *al-Sihah*, a man is described as having *'ubiyya*, meaning pride and tyranny. The *'ubiyyat al-jahiliyya* is its arrogance.]

[This was narrated by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban, Abu Ya'la and Ibn Abi Hatim, from the narration of 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar from Ibn 'Umar. On this subject there is also a report from Abu Hurayra, narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ahmad, al-Bazzar and Ibn al-Mubarak in *al-Birr wa'l-Sila*, from the narration of Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id from his father, from him, similar to it. Some have said, from Sa'id from Abu Hurayra: and from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Qudama al-Hatibi, who said: My father told me that the Prophet (ﷺ) in the year of the conquest of Mecca ascended the pulpit, praised God and extolled Him, then said: "Amma ba'd, O people," and he mentioned something similar, and he (the narrator) recorded it.]

Then he recited the verse. And from him, peace be upon him: "Whoever would like to be the most honourable of people, let him fear God."

[This was narrated by al-Hakim, al-Bayhaqi, Abu Ya'la, Ishaq, 'Abd and al-Tabarani, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilya*, all by way of Hisham ibn Ziyad Abu'l-Miqdam from Muhammad ibn Ka'b from Ibn 'Abbas, more complete than it. Al-Bayhaqi said in *al-Zuhd*: they spoke about Hisham because of this hadith, and that he used to say: "Narrate to me from Muhammad ibn Ka'b," then claimed that he had heard it from Muhammad. Then al-Bayhaqi narrated it by way of 'Abd al-Jabbar ibn Muhammad al-'Attaridi, the father of Ahmad, from 'Abd al-Rahman al-Tayyibi ibn al-Qasim ibn 'Urwa, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, from Ibn 'Abbas, raising the hadith, similar to it.]

And from Ibn 'Abbas: the nobility of this world is wealth, and the nobility of the Hereafter is piety.

And from Yazid ibn Shajara: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed by in the market of Medina and saw a black slave boy who said:

"Whoever buys me, on condition that I not be prevented from the five daily prayers behind the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace."

A man bought him, and the Messenger of God (may God bless him and grant him peace) would see him at every prayer. One day he missed him and asked about him, and his master said: "He has a fever." So he visited him, then asked about him again after three days, and the master said: "He is in his final state," so he came to him while he was in his last breaths, and he took charge of washing him and burying him. Then a great matter befell the Muhajirun and the Ansar, and this verse was revealed.

[Al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi mentioned this in this form without a chain of transmission.]

Faith (al-iman) is affirmation together with trust and the tranquillity of the soul. Islam (al-islam) is entering into peace (al-silm), and it means leaving the state of being a combatant against the believers by professing the two testimonies (al-shahadatayn).

Do you not see His saying, ﴿and faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾? So know that what is verbal acknowledgment by the tongue without the heart agreeing with it is Islam, and what the heart agrees with the tongue about is faith.

If you say: what is the reasoning behind His saying, ﴿Say: You have not believed, but say, "We have submitted"﴾? The arrangement of the words would seem to require: "Say: Do not say, 'We believe,' but say, 'We have submitted'," or "Say: You have not believed, but you have submitted"?

I say: This arrangement conveys first the refutation of their claim and the rejection of what they had appropriated. [[Mahmud said: "The reasoning of this arrangement is the refutation of their claim first, etc." Ahmad said: Similar to this arrangement and attention to this subtlety is His saying, ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say, "We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah"﴾, then He said: ﴿And Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾. Since the implication of this is Allah's refutation of them in their testimony to the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), He placed before that a preface which summarises the purpose and frees it from the calamities and afflictions of doubt, so He said between the two statements, ﴿And Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger﴾, and then after that said: ﴿And Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾. It thus becomes clear that they lied in what they claimed, namely the testimony of their hearts to the truth, because that is the reality of testimony, not that they lied that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is a messenger from Allah. The thing that frees the matter is His saying, Mighty and Exalted is He, ﴿And Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger﴾.]] So it was said: ﴿Say: You have not believed.﴾ In this kind of refutation a fine courtesy is observed, in that the word for lying is not stated explicitly, so it was not said, "You have lied," and He placed ﴿You have not believed﴾, which negates what they claimed to affirm, in its place. Then He drew attention to having put it in place of "You have lied" in His saying, describing the sincere ones, ﴿Those are the truthful﴾, as an allusion that these are the liars. Many an allusion cannot be matched by an explicit statement.

He dispensed with the clause ﴿You have not believed﴾ for saying "Do not say, 'We believe'," because it would be offensive to address them with a wording whose meaning is a prohibition against saying that one believes. Then the clause introduced by the particle of correction (al-istidrak) was joined to it, governed by the sense, and He did not say, "But you have submitted," so that it would come out in the manner of an assumption and a claim, just as their saying "We believe" was. Had it been said, "But you have submitted," its coming out would have been in the setting of granting them their claim and counting their words as valid, and it is not valid.

If you say: His saying ﴿and faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ after His saying ﴿Say: You have not believed﴾ resembles repetition without standing on its own with a new benefit.

I say: It is not so. The benefit of ﴿You have not believed﴾ is the refutation of their claim, while His saying ﴿and faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ is a time-limit for what they were commanded to say, as if it were said to them: "But say, 'We have submitted', since the agreement of your hearts with your tongues has not been established." This is because it is a statement in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿say﴾. What is in ﴿lamma﴾ of the sense of expectation indicates that these people will believe afterwards.

﴿He will not diminish (la yaltikum) you﴾, meaning He will not reduce you or wrong you.

It is said: "Altahu al-sultan haqqahu," meaning the ruler diminished his right severely; this is the dialect of Ghatafan. The dialect of Asad and the people of the Hijaz is "lataha yalituh."

Al-Asma'i related from Umm Hisham al-Sulamiyya that she said: "Praise be to Allah, who is not reduced (la yufat) and is not diminished (la yalat), and whom voices do not harm (wa la tasummuhu al-aswat)." [[Her saying "and whom voices do not harm": if it is from al-wasm, the meaning is: voices do not split him or defame him; if it is from al-summ (deafness), the meaning is: you will not find him deaf. In al-Sihah, "al-wasm" means splitting and defect, and in it "asmamtuhu" means: I found him deaf. (ʿAyn)]] It was read in both dialects: "la yaltikum" and "la ya'talikum." Its meaning is similar to His saying, ﴿so no soul will be wronged in anything﴾.

The meaning of obeying Allah and His Messenger is that they repent of the hypocrisy they had been in, fix their hearts upon faith, and act according to its requirements. If they do this, Allah accepts their repentance, grants them His forgiveness, and bestows upon them His abundant reward.

It is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that a group from the tribe of Banu Asad came to Medina in a year of drought. They professed the testimony, spoiled the roads of Medina with filth, and raised its prices. They would come and go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saying: "The Arabs have come to you with their own selves upon the backs of their mounts, and we have come to you with the burdens and the families," wanting charity and placing him under obligation. So this was revealed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 49, verse 15:

ارتاب (irtāba): it is the reflexive form (muṭāwaʿa) of "arābahu," meaning he caused him to fall into doubt together with suspicion. The meaning is: they believed, then no doubt entered their hearts regarding what they believed in, nor any suspicion toward those whom they affirmed as truthful and acknowledged that the truth is from them. If you say: what is the meaning of "thumma" (then) here, since it indicates delay, and the absence of doubt must accompany faith, because it is a description of it, as I have shown, that faith conveys the meaning of trust and tranquility whose reality is certainty and the absence of doubt? I answer: the answer follows two paths. One is that whoever has attained faith may be confronted by Satan or some misleading people after the tranquility of the breast, so they cast doubt into him and throw into his heart what damages his certainty, or he himself reflects in an unsound manner by which he falls into doubt, then he persists in that, headstrong, not seeking a way out for it. So the believers in truth are described as distant from these destructive sins.

Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Then they remained steadfast﴾ [41:30]. The second: since certainty and the removal of doubt are the essence of faith, they were singled out for mention after the mention of faith, drawing attention to their place, and they were joined to faith with the word "thumma" (then), signaling their settling in extended and prolonged times as something fresh and new. ﴿And strove﴾: it may be that the one striven against is implied, namely the enemy who fights, or Satan, or desire; and it may be that "jāhada" is for emphasis in "jahada" (to exert effort). It may be that striving with the self is intended as fighting (al-ghazw), and that it encompasses all acts of worship together; and striving with wealth is like what ʿUthmān (may Allah be pleased with him) did in the army of hardship (jaysh al-ʿusra); and it may encompass the zakat and everything related to wealth of the works of righteousness in which a man bears hardship with his wealth for the sake of Allah, the Exalted. ﴿Those are the truthful﴾: those who were truthful in their saying "we have believed," and did not lie as the Bedouins of the Banu Asad lied. Or they are those whose faith is a faith of truthfulness, a faith of reality, earnestness, and steadfastness.

It is said: "I did not know of your arrival," meaning: I did not perceive it, nor was I aware of it. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you inform Allah about your religion?﴾ and in it is a charge of ignorance against them.

They say: "He conferred a favour upon him (manna ʿalayhi) with a bounty (yad) which he extended to him," just as you say "he bestowed a kindness upon him" (anʿama ʿalayhi) and "he conferred a benefit upon him" (afḍala ʿalayhi). Al-manna is the blessing whose giver does not seek a return from the one to whom he extends it. Its derivation is from al-mann, which means "cutting," because he extends it only to cut off his need by it and nothing else, without intending to seek a reward. Then it is said: "He reproached him for his act" (manna ʿalayhi ṣanʿahu) when he counts it against him as a favour and a benefit. [The gloss on the phrase "whose giver does not seek a return" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: azlaltu ilayhi niʿmatahu, meaning "I demanded its return from him"; and in the hadith, "whoever has a blessing extended to him, let him give thanks for it," and azlaltu shayʾan min ḥaqqihi means "I gave him something of his right." (ʿ)]

The context of this verse contains subtlety and elegance. Allah called what the Bedouins had (al-aʿrāb, the nomadic Arabs) Islam, and denied that it was, as they claimed, faith (īmān). When they reproached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what they had done, Allah the Exalted said to His Messenger, peace be upon him: "These people count against you something that does not deserve to be counted against you, namely their conversion, which is rightly called Islam. So say to them: Do not count your Islam against me, that is, your conversion, which I call Islam and not faith." Then He said: "Rather, Allah counts it against you that He has guided you to faith by His grace (an amaddakum biwafqihi ḥaythu hadākum lil-īmān), according to your claim and assertion that you were guided to it and granted success in it, if your claim is true and your assertion is sincere. But you claim and assert what Allah knows to be otherwise." The attribution of Islam to them and the mention of faith unattributed to them is something that the reflective one will not miss. The answer to the conditional is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it; its estimated form is: "If you are truthful in your claim of faith, then the favour is Allah's upon you."

It was also read: "in an [if] He guided you" (in hadākum), with a kasra on the hamza.

In the reading of Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him: "since He guided you" (idh hadākum). It was also read "taʿmalūn" with the ta' and with the yā' (yaʿmalūn). This is an explanation that they were not truthful in their claim. The meaning is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows every hidden thing in the world and sees every deed you do, in your private and public affairs; nothing of it is hidden from Him. How then could what is in your hearts be hidden from Him, and your truthfulness and falsehood not be manifest to Him? That is because His knowledge of every known thing is one unchanging state.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Ḥujurāt will be given a reward equal to the number of those who obeyed Allah and those who disobeyed Him." [Narrated by al-Thaʿlabī, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wāḥidī through various chains from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, with this wording.]
